alignment.note: Greek and Latin use a participle (κράξας / clamans, 'having cried out'); the Peshitta renders with a finite verb ܘܩܥܐ ('and he cried out'), reflecting the Syriac preference for paratactic finite clauses over Greek participial subordination. The same Syriac token serves the conjunction of the previous group.
φωνῇ μεγάλῃ / ܒܩܠܐ ܪܡܐ / voce magna ('with a loud voice'); the Syriac ܪܡܐ literally 'high/exalted' is the idiomatic equivalent of 'loud'.

Greek λέγει is historic present ('he says'); the Peshitta ܘܐܡܪ and Latin dixit both render it as past/aorist, a routine tense-levelling. The Vulgate colon (token 5) belongs to this group as the speech-introduction marker.
καὶ σοί / ܘܠܟ / et tibi ('and to you'); the Syriac fuses conjunction and pronoun into a single inflected form ܘܠܟ.

υἱὲ τοῦ θεοῦ / ܒܪܗ ܕܐܠܗܐ / Fili Dei ('Son of God'); Greek and Latin lack the resumptive pronominal suffix present in Syriac ܒܪܗ ('his son'), a standard Syriac construct idiom that does not alter the sense.

τοῦ ὑψίστου / ܡܪܝܡܐ / altissimi ('the Most High'); the Vulgate interrogative mark (token 14) closes the clause. Greek uses article + superlative adjective, Syriac a single derived participle from r-y-m ('to be high').

ὁρκίζω / ܡܘܡܐ ܐܢܐ / adjuro ('I adjure'); the Syriac uses a periphrastic participle plus independent pronoun (ܡܘܡܐ ܐܢܐ, lit. 'adjuring [am] I') to express the first-person present, equivalent to the synthetic Greek and Latin verbs.

Greek expresses the oath-object with a double accusative (σε τὸν θεόν, 'I adjure you [by] God'); Latin makes the instrumentality explicit with the preposition per Deum, and Syriac likewise uses the prefixed preposition ܒ- (ܒܐܠܗܐ, 'by God'). The versions disambiguate the bare Greek accusative idiom.
μή / ܕܠܐ / ne ('that not'); the Syriac ܕܠܐ combines the relative/complementiser ܕ with the negative ܠܐ, introducing the prohibitive clause.
με / (suffix in ܬܫܢܩܢܝ) / me ('me'); the Syriac object is enclitic to the following verb.

Greek βασανίσῃς and Latin torqueas denote 'torment/torture'; the Syriac ܬܫܢܩܢܝ (root sh-n-q, cognate with Arabic خَنَقَ 'to strangle/choke') carries a slightly more physical nuance of anguish, though functionally equivalent. The Syriac form incorporates the first-person object suffix grouped above.
